The AI Stack · Episode 11

The Loop: Follow $100 Around the AI Money Loop

Who pays whom, with whose money, and how many times we count it.

Chipmakers invest in the cloud companies that buy their chips. Many of those are neoclouds, a neocloud being a newer company that rents out racks of AI chips. Neoclouds sign contracts with AI labs that the chipmakers also fund. It's not a scandal and it's not a free lunch. It's a loop, and the loop changes what "revenue" and "demand" mean. We follow one seed of cash around it, lap by lap, and tag every number with how much we trust it.

Toy model, per $100 of seed cash. Nothing here is a forecast, and none of it is investment advice. Promises are never counted as cash.
CHAPTER 01
Start with a dinner table

The $20 that paid for dinner four times

Four friends sit down for dinner with exactly one $20 bill between them. Ana hands it to Ben for a haircut. Ben hands it to Cy for a lasagna. Cy pays Dee for a logo. Dee pays Ana for a guitar lesson. Everybody just made a sale.

Now ask each of them how business is. Every single one will say: "I booked $20 this week." Four sales, four happy bookkeepers. And the only money that ever existed was still sitting in one hand at the end, exactly where it started.

Nobody lied. Each sale was real, each service was done, each receipt is honest. But if you add up the receipts and call it "demand," you've counted one bill over and over. That's the idea behind this entire episode.

Sales are not the same thing as money from outside the table.

What this means

Chapter 2

Meet the loop

Picture a chipmaker that writes a check to a customer so the customer can buy the chipmaker's chips. Fine so far. Companies invest in customers all the time. Now add a neocloud (a newer company that rents out racks of AI chips) that borrows against that customer's contract, a bank that lends to the neocloud, and a promise from the chipmaker to cover the rent if the customer stumbles. Same dollars, many name tags. (A hyperscaler, in the filters below, is one of the giant cloud companies such as Microsoft, Amazon, Google or Meta.) Below is every deal we could source. Some lines are cash that moved. Plenty are only promises. The task is telling them apart.

Deal type
Kind of money
What the deal types mean
Equity (E)
Cash for a share of ownership.
Debt (D)
A loan that has to be repaid with interest.
Compute contract (C)
A promise to rent computing power for years. Not cash until the rent is paid.
Chip purchase ($)
An agreement to buy chips, often over several years.
Backstop (B)
A promise to step in and pay if the tenant can't.
Guarantee (G)
A promise to cover someone else's debt or lease payments if they miss them.
Warrant (W)
The right to buy a company's shares later at a price fixed today.
Lease (L)
Rent paid for use of a building or machines.
Revenue share (R)
Paying a slice of sales to a partner.
Letter of intent (?)
A non-binding note saying two sides plan to make a deal. It commits no money.
Mixed round
One funding round whose money came partly from vendors and partly from outside investors.

The bull reading

Backers point to the fact that most of these lines are written contracts, often with large, well-resourced customers who committed to years of demand before the buildings were finished. They argue that a chipmaker holding a stake in its customers shares their upside, and they point to reports that spending by end users has been growing.

The bear reading

Skeptics point to how many of these lines run back to a small set of names, so that one dollar can show up as an investment, as someone else's revenue and as a backlog number. They note that the dashed lines are promises rather than cash, and they warn that if end users spend less than hoped, many of these lines could weaken together because they lean on the same future spending.

What this means. Read the solid lines and the dashed lines as two different maps. Solid is money that moved. Dashed is an agreement that might. The loop is real. How much of it is paid for by outsiders is the question we'll chase through the rest of this page, and we don't know the full answer yet.

      05
      Who has a claim on one GPU?

      The claims stack

      Picture one GPU sitting in a rack. Now count the people who think they have a claim on it.

      A lender took it as collateral. A bank lent to the lender. Bond holders at the parent company are watching it too. The customer prepaid for its time. A big supplier promised to cover the rent if the customer walks. Somebody owns the equity, and somebody else owns a piece of the customer.

      Same chip. Seven layers of paperwork (some of chapter 3's nine claims are grouped here, so you see seven). Let's stack them up and see what happens when the chip gets older. (Toy numbers throughout, per $100 of seed cash.)

      This is not double-pledging.

      Double-pledging means promising the same thing to two different lenders without telling them. That is not what is happening here, and nothing on this page implies it. Layered claims are an ordinary capital structure. Your house can carry a mortgage, a home-equity line and a contractor's lien, and nobody calls that fraud. Each layer has its own place in line, and everyone can read where.

      The question here is different. Nearly every layer gets paid from the same place: future spending by end users on AI. When claims all depend on one thing, they tend to wobble together. That's the point of this chapter, and it's a point about correlation, not wrongdoing.

        06
        Promises versus cash

        Promises vs. cash

        Say you sign a lease for a very nice apartment. Rent is $4,000 a month, five years, and you've never earned more than $2,000 a month. Is that a lie? No. You might be about to get a big promotion. You might also be about to get a roommate. The lease itself doesn't tell us which.

        That's what a lot of the AI numbers look like right now. A backlog or RPO (remaining performance obligations) is a signed promise to buy something later. It's a real contract. It is not cash in a bank account. So let's put the promises on one side, the cash on the other, and see how far apart they are. We'll draw promises as dashed bars, and we'll never add them to cash.

        Promises and cash, same scale (billions of dollars)

        OpenAI first. Solid bars are money that exists or arrives each year. Dashed bars are promises it has made to pay.

        Years of today's revenue needed to pay the commitments

        Take what a lab has promised and divide by what it earns in a year. It's a crude yardstick, because revenue isn't profit and the promises are spread over many years. But it shows scale. Then drag the slider and let the lab grow.

        Who is holding promises, and who is holding cash

        Backlogs at the companies that build and rent the compute (neoclouds are newer companies that rent out racks of AI chips), next to Nvidia's own commitments. Many of these backlogs trace back to the same few labs, so be careful about adding them up.

          Bear reading

            Take-or-pay versus flexible

            Take-or-pay means you pay whether or not you use the capacity, like a gym membership you can't cancel. Flexible means you can scale back, like a month-to-month rental. A take-or-pay backlog is firmer for the seller. A flexible one is firmer for the buyer. When you read a big backlog number, the first question is which kind it is. Most of the headlines don't say.

            What this means

            Chapter 7

            Who's on both sides

            Imagine your landlord is also your lender, your biggest tenant and a part-owner of your business. In AI infrastructure that is described as a partnership, and it cuts two ways: it lines up interests, and it ties fates together. When two companies sit on several sides of the same table at once, a problem at one of them doesn't stay put. We went through every deal in our dataset and lined up each pair of companies by the roles they play for each other.

            The role letters

              The most overlapping pairs

              Sort by
              The bull reading

              Backers point to how long-term infrastructure usually gets built: a supplier that also invests is putting its own money behind its product, and a customer that owns a piece has a reason to stay. They note that cloud, telecom and shipping all grew up with ties like these, and that many of these links are written into contracts that lenders and auditors review.

              The bear reading

              Skeptics point to how a stumble can travel: when one company is another's supplier, customer and investor at once, trouble at one can pass along all three links in the same week. They add that the ties make it harder to tell how much demand is real, since some of a customer's spending may trace back to its supplier's own money, a share that can't be measured precisely from public deals.

              What this means. One company wearing several hats is not a scandal, and it isn't proof of a bubble either. It's a map of how much would have to go right together. The more roles two firms play for each other, the more their fortunes are one story, and that's the thing to watch when the weather changes.

              08
              Where does the debt actually sit?

              Off the balance sheet

              Think about a restaurant owner who doesn't own the building. A landlord does. The owner pays rent, the landlord holds the mortgage, and nobody calls that a scheme. It's just how restaurants work.

              Now make the restaurant a hyperscaler (a giant cloud company like Microsoft, Amazon, Google or Meta), the building a data center financed by a multibillion-dollar bond, and the landlord a joint venture set up for the purpose. Same idea, bigger zeros. Seven structures keep showing up in the AI buildout, and each one moves debt or risk from one place to another. Each card below has a diagram. Press Next to step through it.

              First, what the phrase means

              "Off balance sheet" usually means the debt sits inside a separate legal entity that the sponsoring company doesn't fully count as its own. That's often legal, often disclosed in the footnotes, and often for sensible reasons. The reader's job is to find the footnote and add the pieces back up. We aren't alleging anything improper in any deal here.

              What this means

              Chapter 9 · The stress test

              What if payments slow down?

              Picture a chain of dominoes. Whether they fall together depends on whether they stand on the same floor. Knock one over and you learn little. Knock them over in a different order and you learn who lands on whom. That's all this chapter does. We take one small cluster from our toy loop (a neocloud, meaning a newer company that rents out racks of AI chips, plus its lenders), squeeze it a few ways, and watch who still gets paid, who takes a haircut (the part of a payment they don't receive), and which promises get called. Then we follow the hit back to where the loop started: Nvidia's revenue.

              What this tool does. You squeeze one small cluster four ways (less customer revenue, cheaper GPU rentals, higher interest rates, a lower Nvidia stock price) and it shows who gets paid first, who takes a loss, and what comes back to Nvidia. It opens on a mild preset, not a base case. Press “Reset to no stress” to see the cluster with nothing going wrong.

              TOY MODEL: not a forecast. Not investment advice. One year, one cluster, $100 of seed cash. Every number below is hypothetical: it comes from knobs you set, not from anyone's books.

                            What this means.

                            Chapter 10 · The history rhyme

                            Is this 2000 again?

                            Around the turn of the millennium, the companies that made the internet's plumbing did something that sounds familiar. Lucent and Nortel sold their gear to a crowd of young phone and data carriers, and in many cases they helped those customers pay for it, through loans and guarantees. A couple of years later, a number of those customers were gone, and so was most of the vendors' stock value. People now line that story up next to Nvidia and the AI build-out. Is it the same movie? Let's put the facts side by side and see which parts match, which don't, and which we just can't tell yet.

                            A comparison, not a prediction. History rarely repeats on schedule. We show what's documented, tag how sure we are, and say “we don't know yet” where that's the truth. No verdict, and no suggestion that anyone today is doing what anyone did then.

                                  EPILOGUE
                                  If you remember one thing

                                  One measure worth tracking

                                  After ten chapters of arrows, here is one question worth keeping in mind: how much of the cash moving around the loop is paid by end customers, the people and businesses actually using AI? It is not the only question, and the number below comes from a toy model whose main default is an assumption, not a measurement.

                                  One number worth tracking: the share of the loop's cash that is paid by end customers. Cash from lenders and outside investors is also outside money, but it is not end-user demand. It has to be repaid or earn a return, and that return has to come from end customers or from someone else's future money. Cash that started with a loop member and came back to it, like a chipmaker's investment in a customer that buys the chipmaker's systems, is recycled. Promises, such as contracts and backstops, aren't cash and stay out of every pile.

                                  A low end-customer share doesn't mean anything is wrong. It tells you how much of the loop still depends on future customers showing up. We can't read the true value off any filing, so we give a range and let you explore what would move it.
